clinicalPearls: Fibroids are benign monoclonal tumours of uterine smooth muscle and are the most common pelvic tumour in women
Many are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, they commonly cause heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, bulk-related urinary or bowel symptoms, and sometimes subfertility
Location matters more than size: submucosal fibroids are most associated with abnormal bleeding and reproductive problems, while subserosal fibroids tend to cause pressure symptoms
They are oestrogen and progesterone dependent, so they typically grow during the reproductive years and regress after the menopause

Treatment is guided by symptoms, fibroid characteristics, and the woman's fertility wishes, ranging from expectant management to medical therapy, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy, or hysterectomy
Medical options aim to reduce bleeding and shrink fibroids, including hormonal treatments and agents that suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
Rapid growth, particularly after the menopause, should raise suspicion of the rare leiomyosarcoma
In pregnancy fibroids may undergo red (carneous) degeneration causing acute pain, and can be associated with malpresentation and obstructed labour
reference.pathophysiology: Fibroids arise from a single transformed myometrial smooth muscle cell that proliferates under the influence of ovarian sex steroids to form a well-circumscribed, pseudo-encapsulated mass of smooth muscle and extracellular matrix. Oestrogen and progesterone, along with local growth factors, drive their growth, which is why they enlarge in the reproductive years and shrink after menopause. Heavy bleeding results from an increased and distorted endometrial surface, altered local vasculature and prostaglandins, and impaired uterine contraction. As fibroids outgrow their blood supply they can undergo hyaline, cystic, calcific, or red degeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma as a cause of abnormal bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound to characterise number, size, and location
Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy to define submucosal fibroids and the cavity
MRI for detailed mapping before myomectomy or embolisation and to help distinguish adenomyosis
Full blood count to detect iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy bleeding
Endometrial sampling when there is abnormal bleeding with risk factors for endometrial pathology
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging uterine mass or postmenopausal growth suggesting leiomyosarcoma
Severe anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding
Acute severe pain from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid
Hydronephrosis from ureteric compression by a large mass
Acute urinary retention from a large or cervical fibroid
reference.prognosis: Fibroids are benign and most women have a good outcome; malignant transformation is very rare. Symptoms often stabilise or regress after the menopause. Recurrence after uterine-conserving treatments such as myomectomy is possible, whereas hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility.
pitfalls: Assuming all abnormal bleeding in a woman with fibroids is due to the fibroids and missing coexisting endometrial pathology
Overlooking submucosal fibroids as a cause of infertility or recurrent bleeding when only transabdominal imaging is used
Attributing a rapidly growing mass to a benign fibroid without considering sarcoma
Failing to consider fibroid degeneration as a cause of acute pain in pregnancy
